messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marilyn had been a widow for six years when the fire came to the apartment building next door, a man-made disaster that turned an ordinary winter evening into something she still described with a painter’s precision. She had been in her kitchen, rinsing brushes in the sink after working on a small landscape, when she smelled alcohol on the stairwell air from the tenants who had been drinking in the hall. A shout rose, then crying, and within minutes the building was filled with smoke, pounding feet, and the frantic movement of people trying to get out. In the confusion, Marilyn was pushed against the wall and pinned for a moment in a way that left her body feeling trapped and folded into itself, as if she were still there whenever she remembered it. What stayed with her most was the look on a young woman’s face as flames licked at the doorway; Marilyn still saw it as if she were looking at a row of photographs, each image fixed and cruel. She remembered, too, the sense that she should have done more, and when the memory came back she was flooded with intense guilt, certain she had failed someone. Even years later, a cry in a hallway or the smell of alcohol could pull the whole scene back before she had time to steady herself, and she would be back in that stairwell with the smoke and shouting closing in around her. The sight of fire on a television report or the sound of pounding feet did not simply upset her; it brought the memory rushing up in such detail that her body reacted as though the apartment next door were burning again.

In the months that followed, Marilyn began to organize her days around preventing that feeling from returning. She stopped watching news reports about fires, riots, or any event that sounded like what had happened next door, and she tried hard not to think about the trauma at all. But telling herself that she should have done more made the memory come back harder, as if the guilt gave it a place to settle and prove itself. The more she judged herself as having failed, the more vividly she found herself back in the stairwell, unable to separate what she remembered from what she feared about herself. When she was alone in her studio, she kept her mind occupied all the time, moving from one canvas to another, cleaning brushes, sorting paints, anything that would leave no quiet space for the scene to intrude. But silence did not stay quiet for long. If she heard crying in the hallway or even at a grocery store, if someone touched her unexpectedly on the arm, or if she caught the smell of alcohol on a passerby near her apartment building, her body reacted before she could reason it out. Her shoulders tightened, she became irritable and snappish, and at times she snapped at neighbors or the clerk at the pharmacy with a force that startled her. The cues felt dangerously close to the disaster, and her vigilance sharpened into a habit of listening for sounds that might mean someone was entering her home, especially at night.

The more Marilyn replayed the event, the more the memory pressed into the present. She could picture the stairwell and the smoke as vividly as if she were staring at a set of photographs spread across a table, and with that vividness came the sensation that her body was back in the same position, frozen against the wall, helpless and braced for impact. After those images had surfaced so often, even ordinary sounds and smells began to feel like warnings she could not afford to miss: a shout in the corridor, a heavy door slamming, or the faint smell of alcohol near her apartment would all make her scan instantly for danger. The memory had made the world feel threaded with reminders of the fire, and Marilyn found herself living as if anything similar might break through at any moment. Each recollection deepened her guilt, and each surge of guilt made the world feel less intelligible to her. She had come to believe that her beliefs about how the world works had been completely destroyed, that safety was a fiction and that at any moment an ordinary hallway, a familiar face, or a smell of alcohol could turn disastrous. What frightened her most was not only the memory itself, but the feeling that it had changed her permanently; she said she would never be able to feel normal emotions again, and that thought settled into a bleak conviction that she was not sure her life was worth living anymore. Those appraisals made every trigger feel more dangerous, so when she heard crying or felt an accidental touch she flinched, anger rose quickly, and she listened harder for signs of intrusion, as though keeping watch might protect her from being caught off guard again.

Over time, the cycle narrowed her life. She slept badly, lying awake and straining to hear every creak in the building, and by morning she was exhausted, more brittle, and more certain that she could not trust what the world might do next. At age 73, Marilyn still paints, but she has become increasingly isolated in her apartment, limiting her errands and avoiding the news, while her studio work has turned into a form of constant self-distraction rather than pleasure. She came for help after realizing that the vigilance, the anger, the sleeplessness, and the dread were no longer passing reactions but the shape of her days. What she hopes for is small but urgent: to stop feeling that every cry, touch, or whiff of alcohol is the beginning of another catastrophe, and to find out whether there is any way to live without the world feeling destroyed.
